title: A Stiff-Necked people
scripture: Revelation 5:1–10; Psalm 149:1–6, 9; Luke 19:41–44; Exodus 32:9; Acts 7:51; John 17:20–26.
theme: The majesty of Christ, the gifts that prepare us for heaven, and our resistance to the peace He offers.
opening: If Jesus has already shown us what makes for peace, why do we continue to resist it? Perhaps the answer lies in an expression found throughout Scripture: we are a stiff-necked people. And yet, even in our stubbornness, God continues to love us.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  You have given us so much, and yet we often struggle to recognize what is right before us. You have sent Your Son to reveal Your love, and through the Holy Spirit You continue to guide us toward the life You have prepared for us.  Lord Jesus, when You looked upon Jerusalem, You wept for those who did not recognize what makes for peace. I wonder how often You look upon our world today with that same sorrow. Forgive us for our stubbornness, our pride, and the times we allow fear or resentment to keep us from loving one another.  Holy Spirit, help us recognize the gifts You have placed within us, whether their purpose becomes clear today, tomorrow, or much later. Give us wisdom to see beyond ourselves, understanding to recognize the suffering of others, and courage to follow where You lead.  Soften our stiff necks and our hardened hearts. Teach us to recognize the love of the Father that Jesus so deeply wants to share with us. May we learn to offer that love freely, as the elders do in heaven, and may we bring whatever peace we can into the lives of those around us.
body:
Today's first reading from Revelation continues John's extraordinary vision of heaven. God holds a scroll sealed with seven seals, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it. No one in heaven or on earth is found worthy, and John begins to weep. Then one of the elders tells him not to weep, because the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has triumphed. But when John looks, he does not see a mighty lion. He sees a Lamb that appears to have been slain.

This Lamb is Jesus Christ, described with seven horns and seven eyes, representing the fullness of His power and the Spirit of God sent throughout the earth. The imagery is remarkable. The One worthy to open the scroll is not presented as a conquering warrior, but as the Lamb who has sacrificed His life. His victory is not measured by the destruction of His enemies, but by the love through which He has redeemed humanity.

The four living creatures and twenty-four elders fall before the Lamb. Each holds a harp and golden bowls filled with incense, which John tells us are the prayers of the holy ones. And they sing a new hymn. I wondered why the hymn was new. Yesterday, the elders praised God for creating all things. Today, they praise the Lamb for what He has accomplished through His sacrifice. Through His blood, He has brought people from every tribe, language, people, and nation to God. Creation is now joined by redemption, and heaven celebrates what Christ has done for us.

But something else in that hymn caught my attention. It says that Jesus has made us a kingdom and priests for our God. I see this as more than a title or responsibility. Perhaps it speaks to how Christ is preparing us for our heavenly life. We are being drawn into a relationship with God that we cannot yet fully comprehend. Jesus wants us to share in the profound love He has for His Father, a love that reaches far beyond our earthly understanding.

We are all invited to that same love, although our journeys are different. The Holy Spirit gives us gifts to guide us, and each of us has our own gifts and abilities. Some we recognize early, others we discover much later, and some we may never fully understand during our earthly lives. We do not know the extent of our potential or the timing of what God may accomplish through us. But regardless of how different our gifts may be, we are all created to know, love, and celebrate the same God. Perhaps our lives are a gradual preparation for the fullness of that love in heaven.

Then we come to the Gospel according to Luke, and the scene changes dramatically. Jesus approaches Jerusalem, looks upon the city, and begins to weep. He knows what awaits Him there, including His rejection and crucifixion. But He also speaks of the terrible destruction that will come upon Jerusalem, a prophecy associated with the Roman siege and destruction of the city decades later. His words are filled with sorrow: “If this day you only knew what makes for peace.”

I find myself lingering over those words. Jesus knows what makes for peace. He has spent His ministry showing us through His teachings and His life: love, forgiveness, mercy, humility, and reconciliation. Yet He looks upon Jerusalem and weeps because the people have failed to recognize the time of God's visitation.

And I cannot help thinking about Jerusalem today, about the turmoil that has continued throughout history and the suffering that still exists. Why does peace continue to evade us? Why, after all these centuries, do we continue to struggle with something Jesus has already shown us?

Perhaps this is where the biblical expression stiff-necked becomes so meaningful. God described the Israelites this way in the time of Moses. It is the image of someone who refuses to turn, who resists being guided even when the direction offered is good. And I wonder how often that describes us.

We can be stubborn in our beliefs, our judgments, our fears, and our need to be right. We can speak of peace while refusing to forgive. We can proclaim our love for God while struggling to extend that same love to others. Sometimes we become so convinced of our own understanding that we resist the very guidance that could lead us somewhere better.

And here is something remarkable when I place today's readings together. In Revelation, the elders willingly bow before God in complete recognition of His majesty and love. Yet here on earth, we can be so stiff-necked that we resist turning toward Him at all. Heaven reveals the fullness of a relationship freely offered to God, while the Gospel shows the sorrow that comes when His love and peace go unrecognized.

Perhaps to Jesus, the way to peace is perfectly clear because He knows the Father's love so completely. That does not mean the suffering involved is simple. Jesus knows the cost of love better than any of us. But He also knows where that love leads, and He wants us to share in it.

This brings me back to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Perhaps wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord are not simply gifts to help us live better lives. They are also gifts that help soften our stubbornness, open our hearts, and prepare us to recognize what God has been trying to show us all along. And the different gifts we receive may allow each of us, in our own way and at our own time, to bring something of His peace into the world.

What moves me most is that Jesus weeps over Jerusalem. He does not rejoice in the suffering that lies ahead. He grieves for the people who have failed to recognize Him. And that tells me something profound about the King we worship.

The Lion of Judah is the Lamb who was slain. The One worthy of every crown is the One who gives His life for us. And the King whom heaven adores is the same Jesus who stands before Jerusalem and weeps.

He knows our stubbornness, our weaknesses, and our resistance. Yet He continues to love us.

Perhaps the question is not why God has failed to bring us peace, but why we so often resist the peace He offers. And perhaps our journey toward heaven begins each time we soften our hearts enough to turn toward Him.
